name: Kodi
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Ghanggo Ate, Yustinus. 2021. Reduplication in Kodi: A paradigm function account. Word Structure 14(3): 312-353. Edinburgh University Press. doi:10.3366/word.2021.0193 (author-deposited typeset proofs, CC-BY-4.0, Zenodo 8084452).
catalog_locator: Sec. 2.3 'Stress', p. 316 (proofs p. 5); sec. 4.1 'Stress and syllable reduplication', pp. 335-339, examples (58)-(65) and Tables 7-10; also p. 322, sec. 3.3.3 ('stress which is mostly penultimate and antepenultimate in Kodi').
catalog_quote: Prominence in Kodi is produced by a combination of (i) greater length (duration), (ii) greater intensity (loudness), and (iii) higher pitch (Ghanggo Ate 2018; Lovestrand and Balle 2019). The prominence of stress in Kodi is culminative in that only one syllable will ever occupy the maximally prominent peak within a stress domain. This means that every word only has one stressed syllable, regardless of whether it is a disyllabic word or trisyllabic word. Stress placement in Kodi depends on the number of syllables. In disyllabic words, stress is penultimate. In trisyllabic words, stress placement varies, and is lexically specific as either antepenultimate or penultimate. [p. 335] First, stress in disyllabic bases is normally assigned to the penultimate syllable and never to the final syllable ... [p. 336] In Kodi trisyllabic bases, stress can be assigned to the antepenultimate or penultimate syllable, and is lexically determined (that is, native speakers learn the stress patterns individually). The final syllable never receives primary stress. ... [p. 337] The stress assignment in derived verbs follows the general principles of stress assignment that was mentioned earlier – namely that stress is penultimate or antepenultimate depending on the number of syllables in the stem.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: One primary stress per word, never on the final syllable. Disyllabic stems: penultimate (= initial). Trisyllabic stems: penultimate or antepenultimate, lexically specified per item (uˈɗoko? no: ˈuɗoko 'kiss', ˈɗoŋgolo 'catch' vs taˈŋaro 'look up', ɓoˈkolo 'big'). Stress is computed on the stem: the productive prefix pa- (causative) is never stressed (pa-ˈhaɣi, pa-teˈrohi); fossilized *ma-/*ka- vary (maˈnduru 'sleep' vs ˈmaɗico 'laugh', ˈkaɓoŋo 'try'). Net effect: a right-edge two-syllable window (penult/antepenult) with lexical choice in trisyllables, penult being the majority pattern.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; the author states every word has only one stressed syllable (culminative) and marks only primary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Trisyllabic stems split lexically between antepenultimate (uɗoko, mbihoko, ɗoŋgolo) and penultimate (taŋaro, ɓokolo); prefix pa- outside the stress domain; fossilized *ma-/*ka- sometimes stressed, sometimes not. Competing formulation: Lovestrand, Balle & Edwards 2021 (APLL13 abstract, citing Lovestrand & Balle 2019) state 'Stress is consistently assigned to the penultimate syllable of the root', and Lovestrand 2021 (NUSA 70: 48) says stressed-vowel lengthening is 'typically the penultimate syllable'; i.e. the non-native fieldworkers analyse Kodi as fixed root-penultimate, whereas the native-speaker linguist reports lexical antepenult/penult variation in trisyllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on elicited citation forms and stems (verbs, adjectives, numerals, the classes that reduplicate); stress domain is the stem excluding productive prefixes; acoustic evidence (duration, dB, Hz) from single-word tokens. Stressed vowels lengthen non-contrastively unless followed by a geminate (Lovestrand 2021: 48).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Kodi = Glottolog kodi1247 / ISO kod (Southwest Sumba); Ghanggo Ate now spells it Kodhi. Ghanggo Ate 2020 distinguishes two dialects (Kodi Bhokol vs Mbangedho-Mbalaghar) and treats Garo/Nggaro as a separate language; his 2021 data are not dialect-labelled (author is a native speaker from the Kodi area, affiliation STKIP Weetebula). Lovestrand & Balle's wordlist data (PARADISEC JL4 / Zenodo 5109673) were recorded in Kodi Bangedo (Homba Tana, Waikadada).

tone_statements.quote: Kodi has contrastive consonant length and phonetic vowel lengthening in stressed syllables. [...] Kodi is not a tonal language, but it has a different kind of phonological challenge. In many contexts, words are pronounced with one less syllable. Kodi people disagree whether the language should be written the way it is pronounced (with fewer syllables), or if all syllables should always be written, even if they are not pronounced in some contexts.

sources.note: Sec. 2.3 'Stress' (p.316): stress cues are duration, intensity, pitch; culminative, one stress per word; disyllables penultimate; trisyllables lexically antepenultimate or penultimate. Sec. 4.1 (pp.335-339) with acoustic tables: final syllable never stressed; prefix pa- never stressed (stress computed on stem: pa-ˈrahi, pa-ɓoˈkolo, pa-teˈrohi); fossilized *ma-/*ka- may or may not bear stress (maˈnduru vs ˈmaɗico); stress 'mostly penultimate and antepenultimate' (p.321).

sources.note: First-hand explicit statement that Kodi is not a tonal language (contrasted with Barayin, which is); Kodi summary gives 5 vowels, 20 consonants, contrastive consonant length, phonetic vowel lengthening in stressed syllables, and syllable-reducing processes (initial/final vowel deletion, metathesis) as the orthographic challenge instead of tone.
